Notes: Year Established = c. 90 BCE: the Machaerus fortress was founded by the Hasmonean king Alexander Jannaeus (r. 103/104-76/78 BCE), the earliest documented Judean presence at the site (a Hasmonean royal fortress with a Judean garrison; no civilian population or count given). One other page (ebaf.edu) attributes the first building to John Hyrcanus; no earlier Jewish presence documented. Event: Hasmonean foundation of the fortress (c. date). Population blank: presence without a count.

Josephus, War 1.8.2-5 (1.160-168): Alexander son of Aristobulus II fortified Alexandrium, Hyrcania and Macherus; after his defeat he surrendered Hyrcania and Macherus to the Romans and Gabinius demolished them (57 BCE). Event: Hasmonean (Judean) stronghold held by Jewish forces and then demolished; no count of residents.

Josephus, War 1.8.6 (1.171-173): Aristobulus II, escaped from Rome, retreated to Macherus with his remaining Jewish force, lodged on its ruins, refortified it 'after a poor manner' and held out against Gabinius for two days before surrendering (c. 56 BCE). Event: Judean (Hasmonean) military occupation; armed followers are a force, not residents. Population blank.

Vörös (Hungarian excavation director): 'The architects of King Herod the Great erected his Machaerus fortified palace in c30 BC ... on the ruins of the Hasmonean fortress of the Jerusalem high priest-king Alexander Jannaeus'; excavations confirmed Josephus on the Hasmonean era and the First Revolt; a Hasmonean cistern was reused in the Herodian period. Event: Herodian re-foundation (c. date). No population figure.

Josephus, War 7.6.2 (7.171-173): Alexander Janneus first built a citadel here, later demolished by Gabinius; Herod as king 'surrounded a large space of ground with walls and towers, and built a city there' below the citadel, with a palace and cisterns on the summit. Event: foundation of the Herodian lower town (Herod's reign 37-4 BCE; Herodian-period midpoint -20 used as the year). Indicates a civilian settlement under a Jewish king; no count.

Large royal mikveh (Jewish ritual bath) excavated in 2016 in Herod's palace (built c. 20 BCE per the page), 'used by King Herod and his royal family'; four mikva'ot in all were installed at Machaerus over almost 100 years, including a modest one used by commoners in the lower city. Presence evidence (Jewish ritual purity practice at the royal palace); c. date. No count.

A mikveh for commoners was found in 1981 in the lower city on the northeastern slope; the caption says the lower city 'was occupied by thousands of ordinary people'. Presence evidence of a Jewish civilian community in the Herodian lower town (dated only to the Herodian/early Roman period; early Roman midpoint 4 CE used). 'Thousands' is a vague popular-press characterization with no method or number, so Population is left blank.

Third season of the Hungarian excavation uncovered a Jewish ritual bath whose pottery belongs to the reign of Herod Antipas (4 BCE-39 CE; midpoint c. 18 CE used); the page calls Machaerus 'the only major Jewish fortress outside Palestine'. Presence evidence (Jewish ritual bath in use under Antipas). No count.

Josephus, Antiquities 18.5.2 (18.119): John the Baptist was sent a prisoner by Herod Antipas to Macherus and was there put to death (c. 28-29 CE, conventional date; Josephus links it to Antipas' later war with Aretas, 36 CE). Ant. 18.5.1 (18.111-112) also says Aretas' daughter fled via Macherus, described as on the border of Aretas' and Herod's dominions. Individual Jew (and Antipas' court) present at the site; c. date. No count.

Mishnah Tamid 3:8: Rabbi Elazar ben Diglai said goats belonging to his father grazed in the mountains/cities of Mikhvar (Machaerus) and sneezed from the scent of the Temple incense. Pre-70 CE condition (1st c. CE midpoint 50 used; approximate). Evidence of a Jewish family's herds in the Machaerus hills; it shows Jewish economic activity in the area rather than proving residence in the town itself. No count.

Josephus, War 2.18.6 (2.485-486): at the outbreak of the revolt 'the multitude of the Jews that were at Macherus' persuaded the Roman garrison to leave; the Romans delivered up the citadel, 'into which the people of Macherus put a garrison for their own security'. Documents a sizeable resident Jewish population ('multitude'), but no number. Event: Jewish takeover of the fortress, 66 CE.

Josephus, War 7.6.1-4 (7.163-209): siege by Lucilius Bassus with Legio X Fretensis (72 CE; some modern works give 71). The Jews 'separated themselves from the strangers', holding the citadel and leaving the strangers (non-Jewish refugees) in the lower town; after the capture of the young Jew Eleazar the Jews surrendered the citadel and were let go. The strangers who fled were 'slain, to the number of one thousand seven hundred' and the women and children enslaved. 1700 is a death toll of non-Jews, not the Jewish population, so Population is blank. Event: end of the Jewish fortress community.

Jewish Encyclopedia (1906), 'Machærus': two years after Jerusalem fell Lucilius Bassus took the fort; after Eleazar was nearly crucified the Jews surrendered on a promise of safe retreat, but the Romans broke it, killing many and enslaving the women and children. This differs from Josephus' text (which says the Jews of the citadel were let go and the strangers were killed). Kept as a separate row because the sources disagree. No resident count.

Event: after the capture by Legion X Fretensis under Lucilius Bassus (71/72 CE) 'The fortress of Machaerus was destroyed and vanished into the oblivion of human history'; the same page says that in 66 CE the citadel had been 'taken over by the citizens of its lower city and later reinforced by the Zealot rebels'. Destruction; the source does not state explicitly that no Jews remained, so Population is left blank rather than 0.
